title: Jeremiah 7:1–15
context: The narrator introduces a word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, who sends him to stand in the gate of the LORD’s house and address those entering to worship (7:1–2). The rest of the unit is the LORD’s message, often called the temple sermon. The people repeat “The LORD’s temple” as a guarantee of safety, but the LORD calls these “lying words” (7:4, 7:8): the temple offers no protection to those who oppress the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, shed innocent blood, steal, murder, commit adultery, and follow other gods, and then say “We are delivered” (7:5–10). The house has become “a den of robbers” in their eyes (7:11). The LORD points them to Shiloh, where he caused his name to dwell at first, and warns that he will do to this house as he did there (7:12–14; compare Joshua 18:1, 1 Samuel 4, and Psalm 78:60). Jeremiah 26 reports a similar message spoken in the court of the LORD’s house, with the threat that “this house” will be “like Shiloh” (26:6); this page names the parallel without deciding how the two accounts relate. The issue is false security, not the value of buildings. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s presence among his people is a gift, not a guarantee that excuses injustice.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the message is presented as the LORD’s, with Jeremiah as messenger. The prophet’s authority rests on the word given to him, not on his own insight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the message comes from the LORD and that Jeremiah is sent with it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a divine word delivered by a prophet, and both receive what follows as God’s message to his people.

verses.text: “Stand in the gate of the LORD’s house, and proclaim this word there, and say, ‘Hear the LORD’s word, all you of Judah, who enter in at these gates to worship the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah is to stand in the gate of the LORD’s house and address worshipers. Arminian readers note the public setting. The warning is given to people in the act of worship, which makes its challenge to their security all the sharper.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the word meets the people at the very place where they feel safest. Shared ground: both traditions read the setting as significant, since the message confronts religious practice that has become separated from obedience.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: “Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place.” Arminian readers emphasize the genuine call and the conditional promise. The people are invited to change, and their response matters for what follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the sincere call to amendment and the promise attached to it, while holding that God works repentance where it occurs. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a real summons to turn, with a real promise of dwelling in the land.

verses.text: Don’t trust in lying words, saying, ‘The LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple, are these.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t trust in lying words, saying, ‘The LORD’s temple…’” Arminian readers note the repeated slogan as false security. The temple is not condemned as a building; what is condemned is trusting it as a guarantee while ignoring God’s commands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the slogan as presumption that turns God’s gift into a charm. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the issue is false security, not the worth of the temple, and both warn against trusting religious institutions in place of faithfulness.

verses.text: For if you thoroughly amend your ways and your doings, if you thoroughly execute justice between a man and his neighbor;
verses.arminianNotes: God says, “if you thoroughly amend your ways and your doings… execute justice.” Arminian readers note that true amendment is concrete. It is measured by justice between neighbors, not by the frequency of attendance at the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see justice between neighbors as the fruit of genuine covenant faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining worship to justice, and both affirm that God looks for righteousness in ordinary dealings.

verses.text: if you don’t oppress the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, and don’t shed innocent blood in this place, and don’t walk after other gods to your own hurt,
verses.arminianNotes: They must not oppress “the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow,” shed innocent blood, or follow other gods. Arminian readers note the joining of social justice and exclusive worship. Both belong to faithfulness to the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the two tables of the law together: love of neighbor and worship of the LORD alone. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as naming the vulnerable whom God protects and the idolatry he forbids, and neither tradition separates the two.

verses.text: then I will cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers, from of old even forever more.
verses.arminianNotes: The promise follows: “then I will cause you to dwell in this place.” Arminian readers note the promise held out to a people who turn. The gift of the land is offered freshly, showing God’s willingness to bless those who amend their ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the gracious promise and see it as rooted in God’s gift of the land to the fathers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a real offer of continued dwelling, joined to the call to amend in 7:5–6.

verses.text: Behold, you trust in lying words that can’t profit.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, you trust in lying words that can’t profit.” Arminian readers note the diagnosis. The people’s confidence rests on words that sound pious but cannot save them, because they have been separated from obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a warning against confidence in religious formulas. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing false assurance and both apply it to any confidence that rests on outward forms rather than on faithful trust in God.

verses.text: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and walk after other gods that you have not known,
verses.arminianNotes: The people steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, and serve other gods. Arminian readers note how the list echoes the commandments. The people break the covenant openly and still expect protection from it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the Ten Commandments behind the list and see the gravity of the breach. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sweeping indictment of covenant unfaithfulness, and both see the moral law as still binding on God’s people.

verses.text: then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, ‘We are delivered,’ that you may do all these abominations?
verses.arminianNotes: They stand before God in his house and say, “We are delivered,” in order to keep doing abominations. Arminian readers note the presumption: worship is used as cover for continued sin rather than as a turning to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a misuse of God’s house as a refuge for sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning against treating worship or deliverance as permission to persist in evil, and both call for repentance that changes life.

verses.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Has this house… become a den of robbers in your eyes?” Arminian readers note the vivid image of robbers retreating to a hideout. Jesus later uses the phrase “a den of robbers” in the temple (Mark 11:17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the image and its later use by Jesus. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s exposure of worship that shelters wrongdoing, and both affirm that God himself sees what is done in his house.

verses.text: “But go now to my place which was in Shiloh, where I caused my name to dwell at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “But go now to my place which was in Shiloh… and see what I did to it.” Arminian readers note the appeal to history. Shiloh had been a place where God caused his name to dwell, yet it did not escape judgment (compare Psalm 78:60).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read Shiloh as a lesson from Israel’s own past (compare Joshua 18:1 and 1 Samuel 4). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s presence at a place does not protect a people who persist in wickedness.

verses.text: Now, because you have done all these works,” says the LORD, “and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking, but you didn’t hear; and I called you, but you didn’t answer;
verses.arminianNotes: “I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking, but you didn’t hear.” Arminian readers note God’s persistent appeals. He did not leave the people without warning, and their refusal to listen was real and culpable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the patient and repeated warnings of God and the people’s responsibility for refusing them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s long-suffering and the seriousness of persistent refusal to hear.

verses.text: therefore I will do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will do to the house… as I did to Shiloh.” Arminian readers note that the house in which they trust will not save them. The judgment follows their refusal, not any weakness in God’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threat as a just response to persistent sin, and note the similar message in 26:6. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that God will not be bound by a building to protect the unrepentant.

verses.text: I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out all your brothers, even the whole offspring of Ephraim.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out… Ephraim.” Arminian readers note the reference to the northern kingdom’s exile as precedent. Judah should learn from what happened to its brothers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the exile of the north as a warning that Judah has ignored. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the Shiloh warning and as showing that covenant privilege does not cancel covenant accountability.
